# Your first ten customers are design partners

Source: https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-10 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pick early customers for fit and learning, not logo value. Agree a written success test up front, work closely for six to twelve weeks on the partner's real data, and convert the ones that succeed into paying customers, case studies and references. The research on lead users and on failed AI projects points the same way: the partner with the problem badly and now, and a clear measure of success, is the one that teaches you something.

Pick early customers for fit and learning, not logo value. Agree a written success test up front, work closely for six to twelve weeks, and convert the ones that succeed into paying customers, case studies and references. The evidence favours this: CB Insights found 42% of 101 startup post-mortems cited no market need, and RAND's 2024 study of AI projects found that unclear problems, unclear success metrics and missing data were among the main reasons more than 80% of them fail.

The first ten customers do two jobs: they pay, and they teach you what the product is for. A famous logo that never uses the product does neither. A design partner is chosen for the second job, and the first follows.

## Who makes a good design partner

**Has the problem badly and now.** The urgency is visible: a deadline, a cost, a regulator, a competitor.

**Has someone who owns it.** A named person with authority to try something new and time to give feedback.

**Looks like your next fifty customers.** A partner too unusual teaches you to build for one.

**Will let you talk about it** if it works, even anonymously.

The first test has a research basis. Eric von Hippel's work on lead users describes customers who face a need before the rest of the market and gain a lot from solving it. Lilien, Morrison, Searls, Sonnack and von Hippel studied the method inside 3M and published the results in *Management Science* in 2002. Ideas from the average lead-user project were projected to reach $146 million in sales after five years, more than eight times the forecast for the average conventional project run at the same time. Those are projections at one company, but the direction is clear: the customer under the most pressure teaches the most.

The third test guards against the opposite error. Amy Edmondson, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2011, warned that pilots are too often run under optimal conditions rather than representative ones. A design partner that is unusually sophisticated, unusually patient or unusually well resourced is an optimal condition. It will say the product works; the next forty-nine may not.

Avoid the famous logo with no owner, the friend who'll say yes to anything, and the enterprise that needs nine months of procurement before you can learn anything.

| Candidate | What it offers | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead user with the problem now | Specific needs, fast feedback, a real test | Few, if any, at the fringe of the segment |
| Famous logo, no owner | A slide | No usage, so no evidence and no reference |
| Friendly founder or investor contact | Easy yes | Feedback shaped by the relationship |
| Large enterprise, long procurement | Eventual scale | Months before any learning; security review first |
| Unusual customer with unusual needs | Strong enthusiasm | You build for one buyer |

## Finding them

Start with a named list, not a market. For a small team selling to institutions, that's account-based selling at its most basic: 30 to 50 named organisations, researched one by one, each with a specific reason to talk now. Our pieces on [account-based marketing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/) and [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) cover the mechanics, and [segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/) shows how to check that the list reflects a segment you can win.

The warmest routes are usually the ones built earlier in the series: your investors' portfolio companies, your [first hundred community members](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/), and their introductions. The [round run like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) leaves behind a list of investors who know your buyer.

**Web3:** your design partners might be curators, market makers, issuers whose asset you integrate, or wallets and front-ends that distribute you. An asset issuer has a reason to want a new use for their token. That's a partnership with a built-in incentive to promote you.

**AI:** your design partners are teams with a workflow you're replacing. Get access to real data early; a model that works on your test set and fails on their tickets is the most common way AI pilots die. RAND's 2024 report, based on interviews with 65 AI practitioners, named data-driven failures as one of five root causes: organisations often lack enough good data to train an effective model. The MIT NANDA study of 2025, reported by *Fortune*, found that only about 5% of enterprise generative AI pilots achieved rapid revenue acceleration, and attributed most of the gap to tools that did not learn from or adapt to the customer's workflow.

> A model that works on your test set and fails on their tickets is the most common way AI pilots die.

## The one-page agreement

| Section | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| Problem | Their words, one paragraph |
| Success test | A measurable outcome and the date it's checked |
| Their commitment | A named owner, weekly time, access to data or systems |
| Your commitment | Roadmap priority, a direct line to the team, support level |
| Terms | Free, discounted or paid during the pilot; price after |
| If it works | Conversion to paid, a case study or reference, logo use |
| If it doesn't | What both sides learn, and a clean exit |

The success test is the line most agreements leave vague, and it is the one RAND's interviewees blamed first. The report's leading root cause was leadership-driven failure: the people commissioning the project did not convey the problem and the measure of success clearly. Writing the test in the partner's own numbers, with a date, removes that failure before it starts. A shared, dated plan with owners on both sides is also the core of a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/), and the same format works here.

Paid pilots, even at a small fee, filter for seriousness. An AI pilot that costs nothing often gets nothing in attention. Agree the price after the pilot before the pilot starts, so the success-test review is also a purchase conversation. Our piece on [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to set that first price when you have few data points.

## Running it

Weekly check-ins with the owner. Ship something visible every one or two weeks. Log every piece of feedback in the evidence log from [Part 3](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/). At the success-test date, review honestly together: did it work, and what would make it a no-brainer to pay for?

Six to twelve weeks is long enough for the partner to change how it works, and short enough to keep a decision point. If the AI product touches the partner's systems, start the security questions in week one; our piece on [the pilot that survives security review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) sets out what to prepare.

Illustrative example: two partners, one decision

Decision
:   Convert one of two design partners to a paid annual contract and close the other pilot with a written learning note.

Reason and owner
:   Both had agreed a success test of halving manual review time on their own tickets by week ten. One hit it with its real data; the other never connected its ticket system, so the test was never run. Owned by the founder.

What changed
:   The converted partner became the first case study. The closed pilot's note showed that a named owner without system access was not enough, so data access moved into the agreement as a precondition.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage B2B AI company, built from patterns across engagements.

## What you get out

A product shaped by real use. Your first case studies, which are only believable if the success test and the result are both specific; see [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/). References for investors. And a clear picture of who your ideal customer actually is, which is usually narrower than the one in the deck.

That narrowing is the result. CB Insights' analysis of 101 failed startups found no market need was the most cited reason, at 42%. Ten design partners chosen for fit are the cheapest way to find out whether the need exists, and for whom, before the company spends a round finding out the hard way.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pick for the problem, not the logo.** A partner with the problem badly and now, a named owner, resemblance to your next fifty customers and permission to talk about it.
- **Avoid optimal conditions.** A partner too unusual or too well resourced tells you the product works when it may not.
- **Write the success test in their numbers.** A measurable outcome with a date, agreed before work starts.
- **Get real data early.** For AI products, the customer's own tickets are the test that matters.
- **Charge something.** A small fee and a price agreed for after the pilot filter for seriousness.

## Sources and notes

- [Lilien, Morrison, Searls, Sonnack and von Hippel, Performance assessment of the lead user idea-generation process for new product development](https://ideas.repec.org/a/inm/ormnsc/v48y2002i8p1042-1059.html), *Management Science* 48(8), 2002. Natural experiment at one company, 3M; sales figures are projections, not realised results.
- [RAND, The root causes of failure for artificial intelligence projects and how they can succeed](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2680-1.html), 13 August 2024. Interviews with 65 practitioners, mostly non-managerial; the 80% failure figure is an estimate the report cites, not its own measurement.
- [Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing](https://fortune.com/2025/08/18/mit-report-95-percent-generative-ai-pilots-at-companies-failing-cfo/), 18 August 2025. Press report of the MIT NANDA study (150 interviews, 350-person survey, 300 public deployments); definitions of success are the study's own.
- [Edmondson, Strategies for learning from failure](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/53761774e4b0e8c9b2acd2a4/t/629fcc85185ef04c9d2549bc/1654639749195/Strategies+for+Learning+from+Failure.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, April 2011. Practitioner essay drawing on the author's research; hosted copy.
- [CB Insights, The top 20 reasons startups fail](https://www.mobiliseglobal.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf), 2019. Vendor analysis of 101 founder-written post-mortems; self-selected sample, hosted third-party copy.
- The candidate table, agreement and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.
